If \(a=0\) or \(b=0\) then the left‑hand side \(ab=0\).  
Since \(\frac{a^{p}}{p}\ge0\) and \(\frac{b^{q}}{q}\ge0\), the right‑hand side is non‑negative, hence the
inequality holds.  
Equality occurs only when both \(a\) and \(b\) are zero, which also satisfies \(a^{p}=b^{q}=0\).

Henceforth assume \(a>0\) and \(b>0\).

---

### 2.  Weighted AM–GM proof  

Recall the **Weighted AM–GM inequality** (a direct consequence of Jensen’s inequality for the concave function \(\log\)):

> For any non‑negative numbers \(X,Y\) and any weights \(\lambda,\mu>0\) with \(\lambda+\mu=1\),
> \[
> \lambda X+\mu Y\;\ge\;X^{\lambda}Y^{\mu},
> \]
> with equality iff \(X=Y\).

Set  

\[
X:=a^{p},\qquad Y:=b^{q},\qquad 
\lambda:=\frac1p,\qquad \mu:=\frac1q .
\]

Because the exponents \(p,q\) are conjugate, \(\lambda+\mu=1/p+1/q=1\).  
Applying the weighted AM–GM inequality gives

\[
\frac{1}{p}\,a^{p}+\frac{1}{q}\,b^{q}
\;\ge\;
\bigl(a^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}\,\bigl(b^{q}\bigr)^{1/q}
\;=\;a\,b .
\]

Thus  

\[
ab\le \frac{a^{p}}{p}+\frac{b^{q}}{q},
\]

which is the desired inequality.

---

### 3.  Equality condition  

The weighted AM–GM inequality is an equality precisely when the two quantities being averaged are equal, i.e. when  

\[
X=Y\;\Longleftrightarrow\;a^{p}=b^{q}.
\]

Conversely, if \(a^{p}=b^{q}\) then \(X=Y\) and the weighted AM–GM inequality becomes an equality, so the original inequality also holds with equality.  

Therefore equality in Young’s inequality occurs **iff** \(a^{p}=b^{q}\) (or, equivalently, \(a^{p-1}=b^{q-1}\)). The trivial case \(a=b=0\) is included in this condition.

---

### 4.  Alternative convex‑conjugate viewpoint (optional)

Define \(\phi(t)=t^{p}/p\) for \(t\ge0\).  
\(\phi\) is convex, and its Legendre–Fenchel conjugate is \(\phi^{*}(s)=s^{q}/q\), where \(q\) is the conjugate exponent of \(p\).  
By definition of the conjugate,

\[
\phi^{*}(b)=\sup_{a\ge0}\Bigl(ab-\phi(a)\Bigr)=\sup_{a\ge0}\Bigl(ab-\frac{a^{p}}{p}\Bigr).
\]

The supremum is attained where the derivative with respect to \(a\) vanishes:

\[
\frac{d}{da}\Bigl(ab-\frac{a^{p}}{p}\Bigr)=b-a^{p-1}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b=a^{p-1}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;a=b^{\,q-1}.
\]

Substituting \(a=b^{\,q-1}\) gives

\[
\phi^{*}(b)=b\cdot b^{\,q-1}-\frac{(b^{\,q-1})^{p}}{p}
           =\frac{b^{q}}{q}.
\]

Hence for every \(a,b\ge0\),

\[
ab\le\phi(a)+\phi^{*}(b)=\frac{a^{p}}{p}+\frac{b^{q}}{q},
\]

with equality exactly when the maximising relation \(b=a^{p-1}\) holds, i.e. when \(a^{p}=b^{q}\).

---

**Conclusion.**  
For all non‑negative real numbers \(a,b\) and all exponents \(p,q>1\) satisfying \(\frac1p+\frac1q=1\),

\[
\boxed{\,ab\le\frac{a^{p}}{p}+\frac{b^{q}}{q}\,}
\]

holds. Equality occurs precisely when \(a^{p}=b^{q}\) (including the trivial case \(a=b=0\)). ∎

**Chebyshev’s Sum Inequality**  
*Statement.*  
Let  

\[
a_{1}\le a_{2}\le\cdots\le a_{n},\qquad   
b_{1}\le b_{2}\le\cdots\le b_{n}\qquad (n\in\mathbb N)
\]

be two real sequences. Then  

\[
\boxed{\,n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}\;\ge\; \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr)\, } .
\]

Equality holds iff all \(a_i\) are equal or all \(b_i\) are equal.

---

### 1.  Trivial and degenerate cases  

*If \(n=1\).*  
Both sides equal \(a_{1}b_{1}\); the inequality holds with equality.

*If the sequence \((a_i)\) is constant* (i.e. \(a_i\equiv a\) for all \(i\)).  
Then  

\[
n\sum a_i b_i = n a\sum b_i = (\sum a_i)(\sum b_i),
\]

so equality holds. The same reasoning applies when \((b_i)\) is constant.

Henceforth we assume \(n\ge2\) and that at least one of the sequences is non‑constant.

---

### 2.  Algebraic rewriting  

Consider  

\[
L:=n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i-\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i\Bigr).
\]

Expanding the product of the two sums gives  

\[
\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i\Bigr)
   =\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_i b_j .
\]

Thus  

\[
L = n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i-
    \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_i b_j .
\]

Rewrite the double sum by separating the terms with \(i=j\) from those with \(i\neq j\):

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_i b_j
   =\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i
    +\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\ne i}a_i b_j .
\]

Consequently  

\[
L = (n-1)\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i-
    \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\ne i}a_i b_j .
\]

Now observe that for any ordered pair \((i,j)\)

\[
(a_i-a_j)(b_i-b_j)=a_i b_i + a_j b_j - a_i b_j - a_j b_i .
\]

Summing this identity over all ordered pairs \((i,j)\) yields  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(a_i-a_j)(b_i-b_j)
   =2n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i
    -2\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i\Bigr).
\]

Dividing by \(2\) we obtain the **verified identity**

\[
\boxed{\,n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i-
        \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i\Bigr)
        =\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(a_i-a_j)(b_i-b_j)\,}. \tag{1}
\]

Thus the left‑hand side of Chebyshev’s inequality equals the right‑hand side of (1).

---

### 3.  Non‑negativity of the double sum  

Because the sequences are non‑decreasing, for any indices \(i,j\) we have  

\[
a_i-a_j\;\text{and}\;b_i-b_j \text{ have the same sign}.
\]

Hence  

\[
(a_i-a_j)(b_i-b_j)\ge0\qquad\forall\,i,j. \tag{2}
\]

Each term of the double sum in (1) is therefore non‑negative, and the sum of non‑negative terms is non‑negative:

\[
\frac12\sum_{i,j}(a_i-a_j)(b_i-b_j)\;\ge\;0 .
\]

Using (1) we deduce  

\[
n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i-
\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i\Bigr)\;\ge\;0,
\]

which is precisely Chebyshev’s inequality.

---

### 4.  Equality condition  

From (2) we see that equality in the whole inequality occurs iff  

\[
(a_i-a_j)(b_i-b_j)=0\quad\text{for every }i,j .
\]

Thus for any distinct indices \(i\neq j\) at least one of the differences \(a_i-a_j\) or \(b_i-b_j\) must be zero. This forces **either** all the \(a_i\) to be identical **or** all the \(b_i\) to be identical. (A proportional relationship \(a_i=\lambda b_i\) would also make each product zero, but with both sequences ordered non‑decreasing this can happen only when \(\lambda=0\) or when one sequence is constant, reducing to the two cases already mentioned.)

Hence equality holds **iff** one of the two sequences is constant.

---

### 5.  (Optional) Rearrangement‑inequality viewpoint  

The Rearrangement Inequality asserts that for two equally ordered sequences the sum of the term‑wise products is maximal among all permutations. Let \(\sigma\) be any permutation of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\). Then  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_{\sigma(i)}\le\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i .
\]

Averaging the left‑hand side over all \(n!\) permutations gives  

\[
\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\sigma}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_{\sigma(i)}
   =\frac{1}{n}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i\Bigr).
\]

Since each individual permutation sum does not exceed \(\sum a_i b_i\), we obtain  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i\;\ge\;\frac{1}{n}
   \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i\Bigr),
\]

which after multiplication by \(n\) is exactly Chebyshev’s inequality.

---

**Conclusion.**  
For any two non‑decreasing real sequences the inequality  

\[
n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i\ge\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\Bigr)
                         \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i\Bigr)
\]

holds. Equality occurs precisely when all the \(a_i\) are equal or all the \(b_i\) are equal. ∎

     \[

     \[

     \]

**Theorem (Cauchy–Schwarz).**  
For any real numbers \(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n}\) and \(b_{1},\dots ,b_{n}\),

\[
\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i\bigr)^{2}\;\le\;\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i^{2}\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i^{2}\bigr).
\]

*Proof.*

1. **Construction of a non‑negative quadratic.**  
   Define  

   \[
   f(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_i-t b_i)^{2},\qquad t\in\mathbb R .
   \]

   Each term \((a_i-t b_i)^{2}\) is a square of a real number; hence \(f(t)\ge 0\) for every real \(t\).

2. **Algebraic expansion.**  
   Using \((x-y)^{2}=x^{2}-2xy+y^{2}\) and the linearity of the summation,

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   f(t)&=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(a_i^{2}-2t a_i b_i+t^{2}b_i^{2}\bigr)  \\
       &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i^{2}-2t\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i
         +t^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i^{2}.
   \end{aligned}
   \]

   The correctness of this expansion was verified with the tool `check_proof_step`, which confirmed that the difference between the left‑hand side and the right‑hand side simplifies to zero.

   Hence

   \[
   f(t)=\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i^{2}\bigr)t^{2}
        -2\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i\bigr)t
        +\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i^{2}.
   \tag{1}
   \]

3. **Applying the discriminant condition.**  
   The expression in (1) is a quadratic polynomial in \(t\) with leading coefficient  

   \[
   A=\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i^{2}\ge 0 .
   \]

   Since \(f(t)\ge 0\) for all \(t\in\mathbb R\), the discriminant of this quadratic must be non‑positive (otherwise the parabola would attain negative values). The discriminant is

   \[
   \Delta =\bigl(-2\sum a_i b_i\bigr)^{2}
            -4\bigl(\sum b_i^{2}\bigr)\bigl(\sum a_i^{2}\bigr)
          =4\Bigl[(\sum a_i b_i)^{2}
                 -(\sum a_i^{2})(\sum b_i^{2})\Bigr].
   \]

   Therefore \(\Delta\le 0\) is equivalent to  

   \[
   (\sum a_i b_i)^{2}\le (\sum a_i^{2})(\sum b_i^{2}).
   \tag{2}
   \]

   The algebraic equivalence of \(\Delta\le0\) and (2) was also validated with `check_proof_step`.

4. **Degenerate cases.**  

   - If \(\sum a_i^{2}=0\), then each \(a_i=0\). Both sides of (2) equal \(0\), so equality holds.
   - If \(\sum b_i^{2}=0\), then each \(b_i=0\) and again (2) reduces to \(0\le0\).

   In either situation the quadratic \(f(t)\) becomes the constant \(\sum a_i^{2}\) (or \(\sum b_i^{2}\)), which is non‑negative, so the argument remains valid.

5. **Equality condition.**  
   Equality in (2) occurs exactly when \(\Delta=0\). For a quadratic with non‑negative leading coefficient, \(\Delta=0\) means the polynomial has a single (double) real root; i.e. there exists a real number \(\lambda\) such that the expression inside the sum vanishes for that \(t=\lambda\):

   \[
   a_i-\lambda b_i =0\qquad\text{for all }i.
   \]

   Hence  

   \[
   a_i = \lambda\, b_i\quad (i=1,\dots ,n).
   \tag{3}
   \]

   Conversely, if (3) holds for some \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) (including \(\lambda=0\) when one vector is the zero vector), then

   \[
   \sum a_i b_i = \lambda\sum b_i^{2},\qquad
   \sum a_i^{2}= \lambda^{2}\sum b_i^{2},
   \]

   and substituting into (2) yields equality. Thus (3) characterises precisely the case of equality.

*Conclusion.*  
For all real sequences \((a_i)_{i=1}^{n}\) and \((b_i)_{i=1}^{n}\),

\[
\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i\bigr)^{2}\le
\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i^{2}\bigr)
\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i^{2}\bigr),
\]

with equality if and only if the two vectors are linearly dependent, i.e. there exists \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) such that \(a_i=\lambda b_i\) for every index \(i\) (including the trivial case where one of the vectors is the zero vector). ∎

kwargs.problem_statement: For a non-negative random variable X and a > 0, prove that: P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X]/a
kwargs.proof_plan:
1. **State the setting and handle trivial/degenerate cases**  
   - Verify that the inequality is vacuous for \(a\le 0\) (since the event \(\{X\ge a\}\) is certain and the right‑hand side is non‑negative).  
   - Assume \(a>0\) from now on.  
   - Note the degenerate case \(X\equiv 0\) a.s.; then both sides are zero and the inequality holds with equality.

2. **Introduce the indicator (characteristic) function**  
   - Define the indicator of the event \(\{X\ge a\}\):
     \[
     \mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}(\omega)=
     \begin{cases}
     1, & X(\omega)\ge a,\\[2mm]
     0, & X(\omega)< a .
     \end{cases}
     \]

3. **Establish a pointwise bound using the non‑negativity of \(X\)**  
   - For every \(\omega\) we have
     \[
     \mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}(\omega)\; \le\; \frac{X(\omega)}{a}.
     \]
     *Justification*:  
     – If \(X(\omega)<a\) then the left‑hand side is \(0\) and the inequality is trivial.  
     – If \(X(\omega)\ge a\) then \(\frac{X(\omega)}{a}\ge 1\), so the inequality also holds.

4. **Take expectations (Lebesgue integrals) on both sides**  
   - Use the **monotonicity of the integral** (if \(f\le g\) a.s., then \(\mathbb E[f]\le\mathbb E[g]\)).  
   - Apply **linearity of expectation** to the right‑hand side:
     \[
     \mathbb{E}\!\big[\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}\big]\;\le\; \frac{1}{a}\,\mathbb{E}[X].
     \]

5. **Identify the left‑hand side with the probability of the event**  
   - By the **definition of expectation of an indicator**, \(\mathbb{E}\!\big[\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}\big]=\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\).  
   - Hence obtain Markov’s inequality:
     \[
     \boxed{\;\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\;\le\;\frac{\mathbb{E}[X]}{a}\;}.
     \]

6. **Determine the equality conditions**  
   - Equality in the monotonicity step occurs iff \(\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}} = X/a\) almost surely.  
   - This forces
     \[
     X(\omega)=
     \begin{cases}
     a, & \text{if } X(\omega)\ge a,\\[2mm]
     0, & \text{if } X(\omega)< a,
     \end{cases}
     \quad\text{a.s.}
     \]
   - Equivalently, equality holds precisely when \(X\) takes only the two values \(0\) and \(a\) (with arbitrary probabilities) and no other positive values; i.e.,
     \[
     \mathbb{P}(X=0)+\mathbb{P}(X=a)=1.
     \]
   - The trivial case \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)=0\) (so both sides are zero) also satisfies equality.

7. **Summarize**  
   - Restate the final inequality, the required hypotheses (non‑negative \(X\), \(a>0\)), the handling of edge cases, and the full description of when equality occurs.

**Theorem (Markov’s inequality).**  
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space and let  
\(X:\Omega\to[0,\infty]\) be a non‑negative random variable (i.e. \(X(\omega)\ge 0\) for all \(\omega\in\Omega\)).  
For any real number \(a>0\),

\[
\mathbb P\!\bigl(X\ge a\bigr)\;\le\;\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.
\]

---

### 1.  Trivial and degenerate cases  

*If \(a\le 0\).*  
Since \(X\ge0\) a.s., the event \(\{X\ge a\}\) is the whole space \(\Omega\); thus \(\mathbb P(X\ge a)=1\).  
The right–hand side \(\mathbb E[X]/a\) is non‑negative and possibly infinite, but the inequality
\(1\le \mathbb E[X]/a\) holds vacuously because the denominator is non‑positive.  
Hence the statement is only non‑trivial for \(a>0\); from now on we assume \(a>0\).

*If \(X\equiv0\) a.s.* (the zero random variable).  
Then \(\mathbb E[X]=0\) and \(\mathbb P(X\ge a)=0\) for every \(a>0\).  
Consequently the inequality holds with equality.

Henceforth we assume \(a>0\) and \(X\) is an arbitrary non‑negative random variable (not identically zero).

---

### 2.  Indicator of the event \(\{X\ge a\}\)

Define the indicator (characteristic) function of the set \(\{X\ge a\}\) by  

\[
\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
1, & X(\omega)\ge a,\\[2mm]
0, & X(\omega)< a .
\end{cases}
\qquad(\omega\in\Omega).
\]

The function \(\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}\) is measurable because \(\{X\ge a\}\in\mathcal F\).

---

### 3.  Pointwise bound  

For every \(\omega\in\Omega\),

\[
\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}(\omega)\;\le\;\frac{X(\omega)}{a}. \tag{1}
\]

**Proof of (1).**  
- If \(X(\omega)<a\), then the left‑hand side equals \(0\) while the right‑hand side is non‑negative; thus \(0\le X(\omega)/a\).  
- If \(X(\omega)\ge a\), then \(X(\omega)/a\ge 1\); hence \(1\le X(\omega)/a\).  

Both cases use only the assumptions \(X(\omega)\ge0\) and \(a>0\). ∎

---

### 4.  Taking expectations  

Because inequality (1) holds pointwise, the **monotonicity of the Lebesgue integral** (or of expectation) yields  

\[
\mathbb E\!\bigl[\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}\bigr]\;\le\;\mathbb E\!\Bigl[\frac{X}{a}\Bigr].
\]

The constant \(1/a\) can be pulled out of the expectation by the **linearity of expectation**:

\[
\mathbb E\!\bigl[\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}\bigr]\;\le\;\frac{1}{a}\,\mathbb E[X]. \tag{2}
\]

---

### 5.  Identification of the left‑hand side  

For any event \(A\in\mathcal F\), the expectation of its indicator equals its probability:

\[
\mathbb E\!\bigl[\mathbf 1_{A}\bigr]=\mathbb P(A).
\]

Applying this with \(A=\{X\ge a\}\) gives  

\[
\mathbb E\!\bigl[\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}\bigr]=\mathbb P\!\bigl(X\ge a\bigr).
\]

Insert this identity into (2) to obtain the desired inequality:

\[
\boxed{\;\mathbb P\!\bigl(X\ge a\bigr)\;\le\;\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}\;}.
\]

---

### 6.  Equality conditions  

Equality in Markov’s inequality can occur only if **every** inequality used in the proof is an equality.

1. **Equality in monotonicity.**  
   This requires  
   \[
   \mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}(\omega)=\frac{X(\omega)}{a}\qquad\text{for }\mathbb P\text{-a.e. }\omega.
   \tag{3}
   \]

2. **Solving (3).**  
   - If \(X(\omega)<a\), then the left side of (3) is \(0\); consequently (3) forces \(X(\omega)=0\).  
   - If \(X(\omega)\ge a\), then the left side of (3) is \(1\); hence (3) forces \(X(\omega)=a\).

   Therefore (3) holds a.s. **iff** the random variable \(X\) takes only the two values \(0\) and \(a\) (with arbitrary probabilities) on a set of full measure.  

   Formally,
   \[
   \mathbb P\bigl(X\in\{0,a\}\bigr)=1.
   \tag{4}
   \]

3. **Trivial equality.**  
   If \(\mathbb P(X\ge a)=0\) then both sides of Markov’s inequality are zero, and equality holds regardless of the distribution of \(X\). This situation is included in (4) by allowing \(\mathbb P(X=a)=0\).

Hence **equality holds** precisely when either  

- \(\mathbb P(X\ge a)=0\) (the right‑hand side is also zero), or  
- \(X\) assumes only the values \(0\) and \(a\) (i.e. (4) holds).

---

### 7.  Summary  

For a non‑negative random variable \(X\) and any real number \(a>0\),

\[
\mathbb P\!\bigl(X\ge a\bigr)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.
\]

The proof rests on the elementary pointwise bound \(\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}\le X/a\), monotonicity of expectation, and the definition of expectation of an indicator.  
Equality occurs exactly when \(X\) takes no values other than \(0\) and \(a\) (or when the event \(\{X\ge a\}\) has probability zero).  

All degenerate cases (\(a\le0\), \(X\equiv0\)) have been treated separately, and no step relies on numerical approximation.

\[

\]

The desired inequality is  

\[
n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}\;\ge\;
\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr). \tag{1}
\]

The proof proceeds in several logical layers:

1. **Edge‑case verification** – When \(n=1\) equality holds trivially.  
   If one of the sequences is constant, each term \(a_{i}b_{i}\) equals the same product, so (1) becomes an equality. These degenerate situations will be recorded separately.

2. **Symmetric reformulation** – Introduce the arithmetic means  

   \[
   \bar a=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i},\qquad
   \bar b=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}.
   \]

   A short algebraic computation shows  

   \[
   \sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_{i}-\bar a)(b_{i}-\bar b)
   =\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}
   -\frac1n\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
            \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr). \tag{2}
   \]

   Hence (1) is equivalent to  

   \[
   \sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_{i}-\bar a)(b_{i}-\bar b)\ge0. \tag{3}
   \]

   The left‑hand side of (3) is the (unnormalised) covariance of the two sequences; because the sequences are similarly ordered, the covariance must be non‑negative.

3. **Application of the Rearrangement Inequality** – The Rearrangement Inequality (see “Relevant Theorems” in the knowledge base) states:

   > For two equally ordered sequences (both non‑decreasing or both non‑increasing), the sum of the termwise products is maximal among all permutations of one of the sequences; the sum obtained with the opposite order is minimal.

   Consequently the identity permutation \(\sigma_{0}(i)=i\) yields a product sum that is **not smaller** than the average product sum over all \(n!\) permutations. Formally,

   \[
   \sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}
   \;\ge\;
   \frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{\sigma(i)}. \tag{4}
   \]

   The double sum on the right can be evaluated explicitly: each ordered pair \((a_{i},b_{j})\) appears exactly \((n-1)!\) times (once for each permutation that maps \(i\) to \(j\)). Hence  

   \[
   \frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{\sigma(i)}
   =\frac{1}{n}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
               \Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{n}b_{j}\Bigr). \tag{5}
   \]

   Substituting (5) into (4) and multiplying by \(n\) gives exactly (1).

4. **Equality analysis** – Equality in the Rearrangement Inequality occurs iff the two sequences are *similarly ordered* **and** at least one of the following holds:

   - All \(a_{i}\) are equal (the first sequence is constant); or
   - All \(b_{i}\) are equal (the second sequence is constant); or
   - The two sequences are proportional, i.e. there exists a constant \(c\) such that \(a_{i}=c\) for every \(i\) (the first case) or \(b_{i}=c\) for every \(i\) (the second case).

   Because our hypothesis already forces the sequences to be similarly ordered, the only possibilities for equality in (1) are that **at least one sequence is constant**. When neither sequence is constant, the inequality is strict.

5. **Conclusion** – Steps 1‑4 provide a complete, rigorous derivation of Chebyshev’s sum inequality, covering all edge cases and delivering a precise description of the equality condition.

_store.proof:
**Theorem (Chebyshev’s sum inequality).**  
Let  

\[
a_{1}\le a_{2}\le\cdots\le a_{n},\qquad  
b_{1}\le b_{2}\le\cdots\le b_{n}
\]

be real numbers. Then  

\[
n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}\;\ge\;
\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr). \tag{C}
\]

Equality holds iff at least one of the two sequences is constant.

*Proof.*

---

### 1.  Preliminary cases  

*Case \(n=1\).*  
Both sides of (C) equal \(a_{1}b_{1}\); therefore (C) holds with equality.

*Constant sequence.*  
If \(a_{1}=a_{2}= \dots =a_{n}=a\), then  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}=a\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i},
\]
and the left‑hand side of (C) becomes  

\[
n\cdot a\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}
   =\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
    \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr),
\]

so (C) is an equality.  
The same argument applies when the \(b\)-sequence is constant.  
Hence the theorem is true for these degenerate situations.

In the sequel we assume \(n\ge2\) and that **neither** sequence is constant.

---

### 2.  Reformulation in symmetric form  

Define the arithmetic means  

\[
\bar a:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i},\qquad
\bar b:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}.
\]

Consider the sum  

\[
\Sigma:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_{i}-\bar a)(b_{i}-\bar b). \tag{2.1}
\]

Expanding each product and collecting terms gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma
&=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}
   -\bar a\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}
   -\bar b\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}
   +n\bar a\bar b.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(\bar a=\dfrac{1}{n}\sum a_{i}\) and \(\bar b=\dfrac{1}{n}\sum b_{i}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
-\bar a\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}
   &= -\frac1n\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
          \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr),\\[2mm]
-\bar b\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}
   &= -\frac1n\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
          \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr),\\[2mm]
n\bar a\bar b
   &=\frac1n\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
           \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding these three expressions together yields  

\[
-\bar a\sum b_{i}-\bar b\sum a_{i}+n\bar a\bar b
   =-\frac1n\Bigl(\sum a_{i}\Bigr)
            \Bigl(\sum b_{i}\Bigr).
\]

Consequently  

\[
\Sigma
   =\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}
    -\frac1n\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
                \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr). \tag{2.2}
\]

Thus inequality (C) is **equivalent** to  

\[
\Sigma\ge0.\tag{2.3}
\]

The quantity \(\Sigma\) is the (unnormalised) covariance of the two sequences; because the sequences are similarly ordered, the covariance must be non‑negative.  We now prove this fact via the Rearrangement Inequality.

---

### 3.  Rearrangement inequality argument  

**Rearrangement Inequality (standard form).**  
*If* \(x_{1}\le x_{2}\le\cdots\le x_{n}\) and \(y_{1}\le y_{2}\le\cdots\le y_{n}\), *then* for every permutation \(\sigma\in S_{n}\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}
   \;\ge\;
   \sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{\sigma(i)}.
\tag{3.1}
\]

Moreover, the right‑hand side is **maximal** when \(\sigma\) is the identity and **minimal** when \(\sigma\) reverses the order.

Apply the inequality with \(x_{i}=a_{i}\) and \(y_{i}=b_{i}\). Because the identity permutation gives the maximal possible sum, we have  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}
   \;\ge\;
   \frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{\sigma(i)}.
   \tag{3.2}
\]

To evaluate the double sum, note that for a fixed pair \((i,j)\) the term \(a_{i}b_{j}\) appears exactly \((n-1)!\) times: choose a permutation that sends \(i\) to \(j\) (there are \((n-1)!\) ways to permute the remaining \(n-1\) indices). Therefore

\[
\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{\sigma(i)}
   = (n-1)!\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{j}
   = (n-1)!\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
           \Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{n}b_{j}\Bigr).
\]

Dividing by \(n!\) gives  

\[
\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{\sigma(i)}
   =\frac1{n}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
               \Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{n}b_{j}\Bigr). \tag{3.3}
\]

Insert (3.3) into (3.2) and multiply both sides by \(n\):

\[
n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}
   \;\ge\;
   \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
   \Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{n}b_{j}\Bigr).
\]

This is precisely inequality (C). By the equivalence (2.2)–(2.3) we have also shown \(\Sigma\ge0\).

---

### 4.  Equality conditions  

The Rearrangement Inequality attains equality **iff** the two sequences are similarly ordered **and** at least one of the following holds:

* (i) all the \(a_{i}\) are equal (the first sequence is constant);
* (ii) all the \(b_{i}\) are equal (the second sequence is constant).

Indeed, if both sequences contain at least two distinct elements, the identity permutation is the *unique* ordering that yields the maximal sum, and any other permutation would give a strictly smaller sum; consequently the inequality in (3.2) is strict.

Translating back to (C), we obtain:

*Equality in Chebyshev’s sum inequality occurs if and only if at least one of the two sequences is constant.*  
When both sequences are non‑constant, the inequality is strict.

---

### 5.  Conclusion  

We have verified the base case, treated the constant‑sequence degenerate case, rewritten the inequality in a symmetric covariance form, and proved the non‑negativity of that covariance by averaging over all permutations (a direct consequence of the Rearrangement Inequality). The argument yields the desired inequality (C) for all \(n\ge1\) and completely characterises the equality cases.

\(\square\)

kwargs.problem_statement: For non-negative real numbers a, b and p, q > 1 with 1/p + 1/q = 1, prove that: ab ≤ aᵖ/p + bᵍ/q
kwargs.proof_plan:
1. **Verify domain and degenerate cases**  
   - Check that \(a\ge 0,\; b\ge 0\) and \(p,q>1\) with \(\frac1p+\frac1q=1\).  
   - If either \(a=0\) or \(b=0\), the inequality reduces to \(0\le a^{p}/p\) or \(0\le b^{q}/q\), which holds trivially.  
   - Record these as the base (edge) cases.

2. **Introduce the convex function**  
   - Consider the exponential function \(\phi(t)=e^{t}\), which is convex on \(\mathbb{R}\).  
   - Use the convexity inequality (Jensen/weighted AM–GM) for the points \(\ln a^{p}\) and \(\ln b^{q}\) with weights \(\frac1p\) and \(\frac1q\) respectively.

3. **Apply weighted AM–GM (or Young’s inequality via Legendre transform)**  
   - Write the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality:  
     \[
     \frac{1}{p}\,x + \frac{1}{q}\,y \ge x^{1/p}y^{1/q}
     \]
     for any non‑negative \(x,y\).  
   - Substitute \(x = a^{p}\) and \(y = b^{q}\). Then  
     \[
     \frac{a^{p}}{p} + \frac{b^{q}}{q} \ge a^{p\cdot 1/p} b^{q\cdot 1/q}=ab .
     \]

4. **Derive the desired inequality**  
   - Rearrange the inequality from Step 3 to obtain  
     \[
     ab \le \frac{a^{p}}{p} + \frac{b^{q}}{q}.
     \]

5. **Alternative proof via convex conjugate (Legendre transform)**  
   - Define \(f(t)=\frac{t^{p}}{p}\) for \(t\ge 0\). Compute its convex conjugate \(f^{*}(s)=\frac{s^{q}}{q}\).  
   - Use the Fenchel–Young inequality \(st \le f(t)+f^{*}(s)\) with \(t=a\) and \(s=b\) to obtain the same result.

6. **Equality condition**  
   - In the weighted AM–GM step, equality holds iff the two arguments are equal, i.e.  
     \[
     a^{p}=b^{q}.
     \]
   - Equivalently, \(a^{p-1}=b^{q-1}\) or \(a^{p}=b^{q}\).  
   - Combine with the non‑negative hypothesis to state: equality occurs precisely when \(a^{p}=b^{q}\) (including the trivial case \(a=b=0\)).

7. **Summary of the proof structure**  
   - Edge cases → convex/weighted AM‑GM → substitution → inequality → equality analysis.

**Theorem (Young’s inequality).**  
Let \(a,b\ge 0\) and let \(p,q>1\) satisfy \(\displaystyle \frac1p+\frac1q=1\).  
Then  

\[
ab\le \frac{a^{p}}{p}+\frac{b^{q}}{q},
\]

with equality iff \(a^{p}=b^{q}\) (the case \(a=b=0\) is included).

*Proof.*

---

### 1. Domain and degenerate cases  

The hypotheses are \(a\ge0,\;b\ge0,\;p>1,\;q>1\) and \(\frac1p+\frac1q=1\).

*If \(a=0\):* the right–hand side is \(\dfrac{0^{p}}{p}+\dfrac{b^{q}}{q}= \dfrac{b^{q}}{q}\ge0\); the left–hand side is \(0\). Hence the inequality holds.

*If \(b=0\):* the argument is symmetric and also holds.

Consequently we may assume **both** \(a>0\) and \(b>0\) from now on, which guarantees that all logarithms below are well defined.

---

### 2. Weighted AM–GM via Jensen’s inequality  

Consider the convex function  

\[
f(t)=e^{t},\qquad t\in\mathbb R .
\]

(Convexity follows from \(f''(t)=e^{t}>0\) for all \(t\).)  
Apply Jensen’s inequality to the two points  

\[
x_{1}= \ln a^{p},\qquad x_{2}= \ln b^{q},
\]

with weights  

\[
\lambda_{1}= \frac1p,\qquad \lambda_{2}= \frac1q .
\]

Since \(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\ge0\) and \(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}= \frac1p+\frac1q =1\), Jensen gives  

\[
f\!\Bigl(\lambda_{1}x_{1}+\lambda_{2}x_{2}\Bigr)
\le
\lambda_{1}f(x_{1})+\lambda_{2}f(x_{2}).
\tag{3}
\]

Writing the weights explicitly,

\[
e^{\frac1p\ln a^{p}+\frac1q\ln b^{q}}
\le
\frac1p\,e^{\ln a^{p}}+\frac1q\,e^{\ln b^{q}} .
\tag{4}
\]

---

### 3. Simplification of the exponential–logarithmic terms  

For any positive number \(x\),

\[
e^{\ln x}=x .
\tag{5}
\]

Moreover,

\[
\bigl(e^{\frac1p\ln a^{p}}\bigr)^{p}
= e^{\ln a^{p}}=a^{p}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
e^{\frac1p\ln a^{p}}=a,
\tag{6}
\]

because the map \(t\mapsto t^{p}\) is injective on \([0,\infty)\).  
Similarly \(e^{\frac1q\ln b^{q}}=b\).

Insert (5)–(6) into (4):

\[
ab \;\le\; \frac{a^{p}}{p}+\frac{b^{q}}{q}.
\tag{7}
\]

Thus the desired inequality holds for all \(a,b>0\). Together with the trivial cases \(a=0\) or \(b=0\) proved in Step 1, (7) is valid for all non‑negative \(a,b\).

---

### 4. Equality condition  

Jensen’s inequality is **strict** for a strictly convex function unless the arguments are equal. Since \(f(t)=e^{t}\) is strictly convex, equality in (3) (hence in (7)) occurs iff  

\[
x_{1}=x_{2}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\ln a^{p}= \ln b^{q}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a^{p}=b^{q}.
\]

When \(a=b=0\) both sides of (7) are zero, so equality also holds. No other choices of \(a,b\) satisfy the equality.

Hence the equality case is exactly  

\[
\boxed{\,a^{p}=b^{q}\,}
\qquad(\text{including }a=b=0).
\]

∎

---

**Remarks.**  
* An alternative proof uses the convex function \(f(t)=t^{p}/p\). Its Legendre (convex) conjugate is \(f^{*}(s)=s^{q}/q\). The Fenchel–Young inequality \(st\le f(t)+f^{*}(s)\) with \(t=a,\;s=b\) yields the same result.  
* The inequality is a particular case of the weighted AM–GM inequality: for non‑negative \(x,y\) and weights \(\lambda_{1}=1/p,\;\lambda_{2}=1/q\),

\[
\lambda_{1}x+\lambda_{2}y\ge x^{\lambda_{1}}y^{\lambda_{2}},
\]

which, after substituting \(x=a^{p},\;y=b^{q}\), is precisely Young’s inequality.

**Theorem (Cauchy–Schwarz).**  
For any real numbers \(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n}\) and \(b_{1},\dots ,b_{n}\),

\[
\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i\bigr)^{2}\;\le\;\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i^{2}\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i^{2}\bigr).
\]

*Proof.*

1. **Construction of a non‑negative quadratic.**  
   Define  

   \[
   f(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_i-t b_i)^{2},\qquad t\in\mathbb R .
   \]

   Each term \((a_i-t b_i)^{2}\) is a square of a real number; hence \(f(t)\ge 0\) for every real \(t\).

2. **Algebraic expansion.**  
   Using \((x-y)^{2}=x^{2}-2xy+y^{2}\) and the linearity of the summation,

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   f(t)&=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(a_i^{2}-2t a_i b_i+t^{2}b_i^{2}\bigr)  \\
       &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i^{2}-2t\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i
         +t^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i^{2}.
   \end{aligned}
   \]

   Hence

   \[
   f(t)=\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i^{2}\bigr)t^{2}
        -2\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i b_i\bigr)t
        +\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i^{2}.
   \tag{1}
   \]

3. **Applying the discriminant condition.**  
   The expression in (1) is a quadratic polynomial in \(t\) with leading coefficient  

   \[
   A=\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i^{2}\ge 0 .
   \]

   Since \(f(t)\ge 0\) for all \(t\in\mathbb R\), the discriminant of this quadratic must be non‑positive (otherwise the parabola would attain negative values). The discriminant is

   \[
   \Delta =\bigl(-2\sum a_i b_i\bigr)^{2}
            -4\bigl(\sum b_i^{2}\bigr)\bigl(\sum a_i^{2}\bigr)
          =4\Bigl[(\sum a_i b_i)^{2}
                 -(\sum a_i^{2})(\sum b_i^{2})\Bigr].
   \]

   Therefore \(\Delta\le 0\) is equivalent to  

   \[
   (\sum a_i b_i)^{2}\le (\sum a_i^{2})(\sum b_i^{2}).
   \tag{2}
   \]

4. **Degenerate cases.**  

   - If \(\sum a_i^{2}=0\), then each \(a_i=0\). Both sides of (2) equal \(0\), so equality holds.
   - If \(\sum b_i^{2}=0\), then each \(b_i=0\) and again (2) reduces to \(0\le0\).

   In either situation the quadratic \(f(t)\) becomes the constant \(\sum a_i^{2}\) (or \(\sum b_i^{2}\)), which is non‑negative, so the argument remains valid.

5. **Equality condition.**  
   Equality in (2) occurs exactly when \(\Delta=0\). For a quadratic with non‑negative leading coefficient, \(\Delta=0\) means the polynomial has a single (double) real root; i.e. there exists a real number \(\lambda\) such that  

   \[
   f(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_i-\lambda b_i)^{2}=0 .
   \]

   Since a sum of squares is zero only when each square is zero, we obtain  

   \[
   a_i-\lambda b_i =0\qquad\text{for all }i,
   \]

   i.e.

   \[
   a_i = \lambda\, b_i\quad (i=1,\dots ,n).
   \tag{3}
   \]

   Conversely, if (3) holds for some \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) (including \(\lambda=0\) when one vector is the zero vector), then  

   \[
   \sum a_i b_i = \lambda\sum b_i^{2},\qquad
   \sum a_i^{2}= \lambda^{2}\sum b_i^{2},
   \]

   and substituting into (2) yields equality. Thus (3) characterises precisely the case of equality.

*Conclusion.*  
For all real sequences \((a_i)_{i=1}^{n}\) and \((b_i)_{i=1}^{n}\),

\[
\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i\bigr)^{2}\le
\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i^{2}\bigr)
\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i^{2}\bigr),
\]

with equality if and only if the two vectors are linearly dependent, i.e. there exists \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) such that \(a_i=\lambda b_i\) for every index \(i\) (including the trivial case where one of the vectors is the zero vector). ∎

**Theorem (Markov’s inequality).**  
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space and let  
\(X:\Omega\to[0,\infty]\) be a non‑negative random variable.  
For any real number \(a>0\),

\[
\mathbb P\!\bigl(X\ge a\bigr)\;\le\;\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.
\]

---

### 1.  Trivial and degenerate cases  

*If \(X\equiv0\) a.s.* then \(\mathbb E[X]=0\) and \(\mathbb P(X\ge a)=0\) for every \(a>0\); the inequality holds with equality.  
Henceforth we assume \(a>0\) and that \(X\) is an arbitrary non‑negative random variable (not identically zero).

---

### 2.  Indicator of the event \(\{X\ge a\}\)

Define the indicator of the set \(\{X\ge a\}\) by  

\[
\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
1, & X(\omega)\ge a,\\[2mm]
0, & X(\omega)< a .
\end{cases}
\qquad(\omega\in\Omega).
\]

Because \(\{X\ge a\}\in\mathcal F\), this function is measurable.

---

### 3.  Pointwise bound  

For every \(\omega\in\Omega\),

\[
\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}(\omega)\;\le\;\frac{X(\omega)}{a}. \tag{1}
\]

*Proof of (1).*  
If \(X(\omega)<a\) then the left‑hand side equals \(0\) while the right‑hand side is non‑negative, so \(0\le X(\omega)/a\).  
If \(X(\omega)\ge a\) then \(X(\omega)/a\ge1\), whence \(1\le X(\omega)/a\).  
Thus (1) holds in all cases. ∎

---

### 4.  Taking expectations  

Since (1) holds pointwise, the **monotonicity of the Lebesgue integral** gives

\[
\mathbb E\!\bigl[\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}\bigr]\;\le\;\mathbb E\!\Bigl[\frac{X}{a}\Bigr].
\]

The constant \(1/a\) can be taken outside the expectation by linearity:

\[
\mathbb E\!\bigl[\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}\bigr]\;\le\;\frac{1}{a}\,\mathbb E[X]. \tag{2}
\]

---

### 5.  Identification of the left‑hand side  

For any event \(A\in\mathcal F\),

\[
\mathbb E\!\bigl[\mathbf 1_{A}\bigr]=\mathbb P(A).
\]

With \(A=\{X\ge a\}\) we obtain  

\[
\mathbb E\!\bigl[\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}\bigr]=\mathbb P\!\bigl(X\ge a\bigr).
\]

Substituting this into (2) yields the desired inequality

\[
\boxed{\;\mathbb P\!\bigl(X\ge a\bigr)\;\le\;\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}\;}.
\]

---

### 6.  Equality conditions  

Equality in (2) can occur only if every inequality used in the proof is an equality.

1. **Equality in the pointwise bound (1).**  
   This requires  
   \[
   \mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}(\omega)=\frac{X(\omega)}{a}
   \quad\text{for }\mathbb P\text{-a.e. }\omega. \tag{3}
   \]

2. **Solving (3).**  
   - If \(X(\omega)<a\), then (3) forces \(X(\omega)=0\).  
   - If \(X(\omega)\ge a\), then (3) forces \(X(\omega)=a\).

   Hence (3) holds a.s. **iff** \(X\) takes only the two values \(0\) and \(a\) (with arbitrary probabilities). Formally,

   \[
   \mathbb P\bigl(X\in\{0,a\}\bigr)=1. \tag{4}
   \]

   The case \(\mathbb P(X\ge a)=0\) (i.e. \(\mathbb P(X=a)=0\)) is included in (4) by allowing the probability of the value \(a\) to be zero.

Thus equality in Markov’s inequality holds exactly when \(X\) is almost surely supported on \(\{0,a\}\); in particular the trivial case \(X\equiv0\) satisfies this condition.

---

### 7.  Summary  

For a non‑negative random variable \(X\) and any real number \(a>0\),

\[
\mathbb P\!\bigl(X\ge a\bigr)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.
\]

The proof rests on the elementary pointwise bound \(\mathbf 1_{\{X\ge a\}}\le X/a\), monotonicity of the expectation, and the identification \(\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{A}]=\mathbb P(A)\).  
Equality occurs precisely when \(X\) takes no values other than \(0\) and \(a\) (including the degenerate case \(X\equiv0\)).

**Theorem (Young’s inequality).**  
Let \(a,b\ge 0\) and let \(p,q>1\) satisfy \(\displaystyle \frac1p+\frac1q=1\).  
Then  

\[
ab\le \frac{a^{p}}{p}+\frac{b^{q}}{q},
\]

with equality iff \(a^{p}=b^{q}\) (the case \(a=b=0\) is included).

*Proof.*

---

### 1. Degenerate cases  

If \(a=0\) then the right–hand side equals \(\dfrac{b^{q}}{q}\ge0\) while the left–hand side is \(0\); the inequality holds.  
If \(b=0\) the argument is symmetric.  

Hence we may assume \(a>0\) and \(b>0\) from now on, which guarantees that all logarithms below are well defined.

---

### 2. Weighted AM–GM via Jensen’s inequality  

Consider the convex function  

\[
f(t)=e^{t},\qquad t\in\mathbb R ,
\]

whose second derivative \(f''(t)=e^{t}>0\) shows strict convexity.  
Apply Jensen’s inequality to the two points  

\[
x_{1}= \ln a^{p},\qquad x_{2}= \ln b^{q},
\]

with weights  

\[
\lambda_{1}= \frac1p,\qquad \lambda_{2}= \frac1q .
\]

Because \(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\ge0\) and \(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}= \frac1p+\frac1q =1\), Jensen gives  

\[
f\!\Bigl(\lambda_{1}x_{1}+\lambda_{2}x_{2}\Bigr)
\le
\lambda_{1}f(x_{1})+\lambda_{2}f(x_{2}).
\tag{1}
\]

Writing the weights explicitly,

\[
e^{\frac1p\ln a^{p}+\frac1q\ln b^{q}}
\le
\frac1p\,e^{\ln a^{p}}+\frac1q\,e^{\ln b^{q}} .
\tag{2}
\]

---

### 3. Simplification  

For any positive number \(x\) we have \(e^{\ln x}=x\). Moreover,

\[
e^{\frac1p\ln a^{p}} = a,\qquad
e^{\frac1q\ln b^{q}} = b,
\]

since \(\frac1p\ln a^{p}= \ln a\) and \(\frac1q\ln b^{q}= \ln b\).  
Substituting these equalities into (2) yields  

\[
ab \;\le\; \frac{a^{p}}{p}+\frac{b^{q}}{q}.
\tag{3}
\]

Thus the desired inequality holds for all \(a,b>0\). Together with the trivial cases \(a=0\) or \(b=0\) proved in Step 1, (3) is valid for all non‑negative \(a,b\).

---

### 4. Equality condition  

For a strictly convex function, Jensen’s inequality is an equality **iff** the arguments are equal. Hence equality in (1) (and therefore in (3)) occurs exactly when  

\[
x_{1}=x_{2}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\ln a^{p}= \ln b^{q}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a^{p}=b^{q}.
\]

When \(a=b=0\) both sides of (3) are zero, so equality also holds. No other choices of \((a,b)\) give equality.

Consequently the equality case is precisely  

\[
a^{p}=b^{q}\qquad(\text{including }a=b=0).
\]

∎

---

**Remark.**  The same inequality follows from the Fenchel–Young inequality for the convex function \(t\mapsto t^{p}/p\) whose Legendre transform is \(s\mapsto s^{q}/q\).

**Theorem (Chebyshev’s sum inequality).**  
Let  

\[
a_{1}\le a_{2}\le\cdots\le a_{n},\qquad  
b_{1}\le b_{2}\le\cdots\le b_{n}
\]

be real numbers. Then  

\[
n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}\;\ge\;
\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr). \tag{C}
\]

Equality holds iff at least one of the two sequences is constant.

*Proof.*

---

### 1.  Preliminary cases  

*Case \(n=1\).*  
Both sides of (C) equal \(a_{1}b_{1}\); therefore (C) holds with equality.

*Constant sequence.*  
If \(a_{1}=a_{2}= \dots =a_{n}=a\), then  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}=a\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i},
\]
and the left‑hand side of (C) becomes  

\[
n\cdot a\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}
   =\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
    \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr),
\]

so (C) is an equality.  
The same argument applies when the \(b\)-sequence is constant.  
Hence the theorem is true for these degenerate situations.

In the sequel we assume \(n\ge2\) and that **neither** sequence is constant.

---

### 2.  Reformulation in symmetric form  

Define the arithmetic means  

\[
\bar a:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i},\qquad
\bar b:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}.
\]

Consider the sum  

\[
\Sigma:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_{i}-\bar a)(b_{i}-\bar b). \tag{2.1}
\]

Expanding each product and collecting terms gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma
&=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}
   -\bar a\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}
   -\bar b\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}
   +n\bar a\bar b.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(\bar a=\dfrac{1}{n}\sum a_{i}\) and \(\bar b=\dfrac{1}{n}\sum b_{i}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
-\bar a\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}
   &= -\frac1n\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
          \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr),\\[2mm]
-\bar b\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}
   &= -\frac1n\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
          \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr),\\[2mm]
n\bar a\bar b
   &=\frac1n\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
           \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding these three expressions together yields  

\[
-\bar a\sum b_{i}-\bar b\sum a_{i}+n\bar a\bar b
   =-\frac1n\Bigl(\sum a_{i}\Bigr)
            \Bigl(\sum b_{i}\Bigr).
\]

Consequently  

\[
\Sigma
   =\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}
    -\frac1n\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
                \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}\Bigr). \tag{2.2}
\]

Thus inequality (C) is **equivalent** to  

\[
\Sigma\ge0.\tag{2.3}
\]

The quantity \(\Sigma\) is the (unnormalised) covariance of the two sequences; because the sequences are similarly ordered, the covariance must be non‑negative.  We now prove this fact via the Rearrangement Inequality.

---

### 3.  Rearrangement inequality argument  

**Rearrangement Inequality (standard form).**  
*If* \(x_{1}\le x_{2}\le\cdots\le x_{n}\) and \(y_{1}\le y_{2}\le\cdots\le y_{n}\), *then* for every permutation \(\sigma\in S_{n}\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}
   \;\ge\;
   \sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{\sigma(i)}.
\tag{3.1}
\]

Moreover, the right‑hand side is **maximal** when \(\sigma\) is the identity and **minimal** when \(\sigma\) reverses the order.

Apply the inequality with \(x_{i}=a_{i}\) and \(y_{i}=b_{i}\). Because the identity permutation gives the maximal possible sum, we have  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}
   \;\ge\;
   \frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{\sigma(i)}.
   \tag{3.2}
\]

To evaluate the double sum, note that for a fixed pair \((i,j)\) the term \(a_{i}b_{j}\) appears exactly \((n-1)!\) times: choose a permutation that sends \(i\) to \(j\) (there are \((n-1)!\) ways to permute the remaining \(n-1\) indices). Therefore

\[
\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{\sigma(i)}
   = (n-1)!\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{j}
   = (n-1)!\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
           \Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{n}b_{j}\Bigr).
\]

Dividing by \(n!\) gives  

\[
\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{\sigma(i)}
   =\frac1{n}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
               \Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{n}b_{j}\Bigr). \tag{3.3}
\]

Insert (3.3) into (3.2) and multiply both sides by \(n\):

\[
n\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}
   \;\ge\;
   \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\Bigr)
   \Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{n}b_{j}\Bigr),
\]

which is precisely inequality (C). By the equivalence (2.2)–(2.3) we have also shown \(\Sigma\ge0\).

---

### 4.  Equality conditions  

The Rearrangement Inequality attains equality **iff** the two sequences are similarly ordered **and** at least one of the following holds:

* (i) all the \(a_{i}\) are equal (the first sequence is constant);
* (ii) all the \(b_{i}\) are equal (the second sequence is constant).

Indeed, if both sequences contain at least two distinct elements, the identity permutation is the *unique* ordering that yields the maximal sum, and any other permutation gives a strictly smaller sum; consequently the inequality in (3.2) is strict.  

Thus equality in Chebyshev’s sum inequality occurs **iff** at least one of the two sequences is constant. When both sequences are non‑constant the inequality is strict.

---

### 5.  Conclusion  

We have verified the base case, treated the constant‑sequence degenerate case, rewritten the inequality in a symmetric covariance form, and proved the non‑negativity of that covariance by averaging over all permutations (a direct consequence of the Rearrangement Inequality). The argument yields the desired inequality (C) for all \(n\ge1\) and completely characterises the equality cases.

\(\square\)

kwargs.problem_statement: For a convex function f and real numbers x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ with weights λᵢ ≥ 0 where ∑λᵢ = 1, prove that: f(∑λᵢxᵢ) ≤ ∑λᵢf(xᵢ)
kwargs.proof_plan:
1. **Verify the degenerate case** – If all weights are zero except one (i.e. there exists j with λ_j = 1 and λ_i = 0 for i ≠ j), then the convex combination reduces to a single point:  
   \[
   \sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i x_i = x_j ,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i f(x_i)=f(x_j).
   \]  
   Hence the inequality becomes \(f(x_j)\le f(x_j)\), which holds with equality.  
   Also note that if all λ_i = 0 (impossible because they sum to 1) the statement is vacuous; therefore we may assume at least one λ_i > 0.

2. **Base case \(n=2\)** – Apply directly the definition of convexity with \(t=\lambda_1\) (so \(1-t=\lambda_2\)):  
   \[
   f(\lambda_1 x_1 + \lambda_2 x_2) \le \lambda_1 f(x_1)+\lambda_2 f(x_2).
   \]  
   This establishes Jensen’s inequality for two points.

3. **Inductive hypothesis** – Assume Jensen’s inequality holds for any convex combination of \(k\) points, i.e. for any non‑negative weights \(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_k\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mu_i=1\):
   \[
   f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mu_i x_i\right) \le \sum_{i=1}^{k}\mu_i f(x_i).
   \]

4. **Inductive step: from \(k\) to \(k+1\) points**  
   a. Let \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{k+1}\) be the given weights with total 1. Set  
      \[
      \alpha = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i \quad (\text{so } \alpha\in[0,1]),\qquad 
      \beta = \lambda_{k+1}=1-\alpha .
      \]  
      If \(\alpha=0\) we are back to the degenerate case handled in step 1. Otherwise \(\alpha>0\).  

   b. Form the intermediate point  
      \[
      y = \frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i x_i,
      \]  
      which is a convex combination of the first \(k\) points (its coefficients \(\lambda_i/\alpha\) sum to 1).

   c. Apply the convexity definition to the pair \((y,x_{k+1})\) with weight \(\alpha\):
      \[
      f\bigl(\alpha y + \beta x_{k+1}\bigr) \le \alpha f(y) + \beta f(x_{k+1}).
      \]  
      Observe that \(\alpha y + \beta x_{k+1} = \sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\lambda_i x_i\).

   d. Use the inductive hypothesis on \(f(y)\):
      \[
      f(y)=f\!\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i x_i\right)
      \le \frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i f(x_i).
      \]

   e. Substitute this bound for \(f(y)\) into the inequality from step c:
      \[
      f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\lambda_i x_i\right) 
      \le \alpha\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i f(x_i)\right)+\beta f(x_{k+1})
      = \sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\lambda_i f(x_i).
      \]  
      Thus Jensen’s inequality holds for \(k+1\) points.

5. **Conclusion by induction** – By steps 2–4, the inequality is true for all \(n\ge 2\); together with the degenerate case from step 1 it holds for every \(n\ge 1\).

6. **Equality condition** –  
   a. In the base case \(n=2\), equality in the convexity definition occurs iff either \(t\in\{0,1\}\) (i.e. one weight is zero) or \(f\) is affine on the interval \([x_1,x_2]\).  
   b. Propagating through the inductive step, equality for \(n\) points holds precisely when every intermediate application of convexity is an equality. Hence equality occurs iff one of the following holds:  
      - At least one weight \(\lambda_i =0\) (reducing to a lower‑dimensional case), or  
      - The points \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) all lie in a region where \(f\) is affine (i.e. \(f\) restricted to the convex hull of \(\{x_i\}\) is linear).  
   c. In particular, if \(f\) is strictly convex, equality can only happen in the degenerate situation where all but one weight are zero (i.e. the convex combination collapses to a single point).

7. **Summary** – The proof rests on (i) the definition of convexity for two points, (ii) constructing a suitable intermediate convex combination, (iii) applying induction, (iv) handling the trivial weight‑zero cases, and (v) extracting the equality cases from the equality condition in the definition of convexity.

**Theorem (Jensen’s Inequality).**  
Let \(f:\mathbb R\rightarrow\mathbb R\) be a convex function, i.e.  

\[
\forall x,y\in\mathbb R,\ \forall t\in[0,1]\qquad 
f\bigl(t x+(1-t)y\bigr)\le t\,f(x)+(1-t)\,f(y). \tag{1}
\]

Let \(x_{1},\dots ,x_{n}\in\mathbb R\) and let weights \(\lambda_{1},\dots ,\lambda_{n}\ge 0\) satisfy \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}=1\).  
Then  

\[
f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}x_{i}\right)\le\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}f(x_{i}). \tag{2}
\]

Equality holds iff either some \(\lambda_{i}=0\) (so that the inequality reduces to a lower‑dimensional case) or \(f\) is affine on the convex hull of \(\{x_{1},\dots ,x_{n}\}\); in particular, for strictly convex \(f\) equality occurs only when exactly one weight equals 1.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Proof

We argue by induction on the number of points \(n\).

---

#### 1.  Degenerate case  

If there exists an index \(j\) with \(\lambda_{j}=1\) and \(\lambda_{i}=0\) for \(i\neq j\), then  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}x_{i}=x_{j},\qquad 
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}f(x_{i})=f(x_{j}),
\]

so (2) becomes the identity \(f(x_{j})\le f(x_{j})\).  
The case “all \(\lambda_{i}=0\)” cannot happen because the weights sum to 1.  
Hence we may assume that at least two weights are positive.

---

#### 2.  Base case \(n=2\)

Take \(n=2\).  Put \(t:=\lambda_{1}\) (hence \(1-t=\lambda_{2}\)).  
Since \(t\in[0,1]\), inequality (1) gives  

\[
f\bigl(\lambda_{1}x_{1}+\lambda_{2}x_{2}\bigr)
   \le \lambda_{1}f(x_{1})+\lambda_{2}f(x_{2}),
\]

which is exactly (2) for \(n=2\).

---

#### 3.  Inductive hypothesis  

Assume that for some \(k\ge 2\) the statement holds for every choice of
\(k\) points and non‑negative weights summing to 1; i.e.  

\[
\forall \mu_{1},\dots ,\mu_{k}\ge0,\;
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mu_{i}=1\;,\;
\forall y_{1},\dots ,y_{k}\in\mathbb R:
\qquad
f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mu_{i}y_{i}\right)
      \le\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mu_{i}f(y_{i}). \tag{IH}
\]

---

#### 4.  Inductive step \(k\rightarrow k+1\)

Let \(\lambda_{1},\dots ,\lambda_{k+1}\ge0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\lambda_{i}=1\), and let
\(x_{1},\dots ,x_{k+1}\) be real numbers.

Define  

\[
\alpha:=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i},\qquad 
\beta :=\lambda_{k+1}=1-\alpha .
\]

The algebraic identity \(\alpha+\beta=1\) follows from the hypothesis
\(\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\lambda_{i}=1\); this elementary manipulation was
checked with `verify_arithmetic`.

*If \(\alpha=0\)*, then \(\beta=1\) and we are in the degenerate case already treated in step 1.
Hence we may suppose \(\alpha>0\).

Define the intermediate point  

\[
y:=\frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}x_{i}.
\]

Because the coefficients \(\lambda_{i}/\alpha\) are non‑negative and sum to 1,
\(y\) is a convex combination of the first \(k\) points.

Apply the convexity inequality (1) to the pair \((y,x_{k+1})\) with weight
\(\alpha\):

\[
f\bigl(\alpha y+\beta x_{k+1}\bigr)
   \le \alpha f(y)+\beta f(x_{k+1}). \tag{3}
\]

Observe that  

\[
\alpha y+\beta x_{k+1}
   =\alpha\Bigl(\frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}x_{i}\Bigr)
     +\beta x_{k+1}
   =\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}x_{i}+\lambda_{k+1}x_{k+1}
   =\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\lambda_{i}x_{i}. \tag{4}
\]

Thus the left‑hand side of (3) is exactly the left‑hand side of (2) for
\(k+1\) points.

Now invoke the inductive hypothesis (IH) on the first \(k\) points:

\[
f(y)=f\!\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}x_{i}\right)
    \le\frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}f(x_{i}). \tag{5}
\]

Insert (5) into (3):

\[
\begin{aligned}
f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\lambda_{i}x_{i}\right)
   &\le \alpha\Bigl(\frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}f(x_{i})\Bigr)
          +\beta f(x_{k+1})\\[1mm]
   &=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}f(x_{i})+\lambda_{k+1}f(x_{k+1})\\
   &=\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\lambda_{i}f(x_{i}),
\end{aligned}
\]

which is precisely (2) for \(k+1\) points.  This completes the
inductive step.

---

#### 5.  Conclusion  

By the base case (step 2) and the inductive step (step 4), inequality (2)
holds for every integer \(n\ge2\).  Together with the degenerate case of
step 1, Jensen’s inequality is valid for all \(n\ge1\).

---

#### 6.  Equality condition  

For two points, equality in (1) occurs iff either \(t\in\{0,1\}\) (so one
weight vanishes) or \(f\) is affine on the interval \([x_{1},x_{2}]\).

During the inductive step the only way to obtain equality in (2) is for
(every) the following to be equalities:

* the convexity inequality (3), and  
* the inductive hypothesis applied in (5).

Hence equality for the full combination holds exactly when either

* some weight \(\lambda_{i}=0\) (reducing the situation to a lower‑dimensional
  case), **or**
* \(f\) is affine on the convex hull of \(\{x_{1},\dots ,x_{n}\}\) (so that
  every application of (1) is an equality).

If \(f\) is strictly convex, the second alternative is impossible, and
equality can occur only in the degenerate situation where a single weight
equals 1 and the others are zero.

∎
